summary: Discusses the idea of precedence and pre-emption, where more important traffic gets priority when a network is overloaded. It reviews how circuit-switched and message-switched systems do this and considers it for packet networks.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 794 discusses precedence: deciding which traffic gets access when a system has no capacity for every request. It suggests that an application can keep a TCP connection request pending so it can consider a higher-precedence request while already serving users.

questions: what is precedence in packet switching
how can tcp pre-empt a connection
subtitle: A discussion of how higher-priority users could gain access when network resources are full.

tldr.problem: When a network or host is saturated, it must decide which requests can use limited resources. Different network types handle priority in different ways.
tldr.mechanism: For packet networks, the memo suggests that an application keep an extra TCP LISTEN pending so it can accept a higher-precedence connection and decide whether to end a lower-precedence one.
tldr.outcome: RFC 794 is an Informational discussion memo, not a protocol specification. It describes application-level handling and possible local resource decisions.

today: RFC 794 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC as obsoleting or updating it. It discusses a strategy for handling precedence rather than specifying a protocol.

sections.title: How Precedence Works in Other Systems
sections.content:
In a circuit-switched system, a user keeps a dedicated circuit after acquiring it, even when it is idle. When the system is full, new circuit requests are blocked. The RFC describes systems such as AUTOVON, where high-precedence telephone instruments can take circuit resources from lower-precedence users.

In message-switching systems such as AUTODIN I, the system stores messages and processes them by precedence. A high-precedence message can be forwarded quickly and may interrupt printing of a lower-precedence message at the destination switch.
sections.plainLanguage: Some systems give priority by reserving or reassigning scarce resources. The memo gives examples of a higher-priority call taking a circuit and a higher-priority message being handled first.

sections.title: Precedence in Packet Networks
sections.content:
The RFC says packet-switching systems have little or no storage in the transport system, so precedence has little effect on the time needed to process an individual packet. When a packet network is saturated, however, it rejects offered traffic. Precedence can sort the traffic waiting to enter the system.

More generally, the memo describes precedence as a way to allocate resources when a system is full. The resource may be circuits, a message-switch processor, or the packet-switching system itself.
sections.plainLanguage: In a busy packet network, precedence can help decide which waiting traffic gets admitted. It does not make processing an individual packet faster.

sections.title: An Extra TCP LISTEN for Incoming Requests
sections.content:
The memo proposes a strategy for applications using TCP, without adding a new TCP mechanism except making the precedence of incoming connection requests visible to those applications. Software serving a terminal could keep a LISTEN pending even while the terminal already has a connection. If a higher-precedence request arrives, the application can decide whether to end an existing lower-precedence connection and switch the terminal to the new one.

With several active connections, the application would close or abort the lowest-precedence one and then post another LISTEN. The RFC favors letting the process that interfaces with the terminal make the decision, since TCP cannot create processes for incoming requests and a process is not useful if the terminal is off. Its example describes an FTP process keeping one request pending so it can serve a flash-override request.
sections.plainLanguage: An application can keep one request slot open while it serves current users. If a higher-precedence request arrives, the application decides whether to end a lower-precedence connection.

sections.title: Resources at the Requesting Host
sections.content:
Pre-emption may also be needed at the host that starts a high-precedence connection. If its FTP or TCP resources are already saturated, the operating system may need to know the user's precedence and free local resources, for example by logging out lower-precedence users.

The RFC treats this as a general system issue rather than one specific to TCP. It says precedence could be associated with a user or terminal, and that either TCP or the operating system could make local pre-emption decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: The requesting host may also be full. The memo leaves it to the system to decide how to free resources for a higher-precedence user.
